description: Hey, I’m Amir, an MS CS student who builds full stack apps and 3D games. We’re building a 3D lunar south pole mission planner on real LOLA terrain: compare landing sites by sunlight, Earth visibility and comms windows, stand at any site to watch the Sun and Earth cross the horizon, and auto-rank the best landing dates. Looking for: Three.js/frontend, Python/data, and someone strong in design or storytelling for the demo video. Fast, focused, shipping to win.
summary: Polaris Window is a free web app that works like a weather forecast for Moon landings. At the lunar south pole the Sun barely rises and mountains can hide the Earth, so a landing site only works if it gets sunlight for power and a clear line of sight to Earth for radio contact, and both change hour by hour. We took NASA's LOLA terrain and NASA/JPL SPICE orbit data, worked out the real horizon around 131,000 points near the pole, and turned it into something anyone can use: pick a site on a 3D map, see how much sunlight and Earth contact it gets over the next year, and let the app rank every landing date from 2025 to 2030 for your mission. Our sunlight and Earth-visibility maps closely match NASA's published maps (correlations of 0.990 and 0.992), so the numbers hold up. It's built for mission planners who want a fast first look, and for students and the public who want to understand why landing at the south pole is so hard.
details:
What it does

Polaris Window answers the two questions every south pole mission has to settle: where should we land, and when? Near the pole the Sun skims along the horizon, so one spot can sit in sunlight for days and then go dark, or lose its view of Earth behind a mountain. Polaris Window shows this for any site and any hour from 2025 to 2030:
- A 3D south pole built from real NASA terrain, with shadows that move with the true position of the Sun.

- For every site: how much sunlight (power) and direct view of Earth (radio contact) it gets, the real horizon with the Sun and Earth paths drawn on it, and a 12-month calendar that reads like a weather forecast.

- Find a Landing Date: enter a mission length and your limits (minimum sunlight and Earth contact, longest night, longest blackout). It checks every 6-hour landing slot from 2025 to 2030 across 13 locations, including NASA's nine Artemis III candidate regions, and explains why the top window wins.

- Side-by-side comparison of up to 4 sites or dates, heatmaps of the whole region (sunlight, Earth view, flat ground, cold traps), a lander battery check, custom sites anywhere on the map, a printable mission brief, CSV export, and share links with QR codes.

- Nine short classroom missions for ages 10 and up that open the app at the exact place and date each question needs.

How it works

We took NASA's LRO LOLA 80 m south polar elevation model and, in Python, traced the horizon around 131,000 points (120 directions each, out to 220 km, including the curve of the Moon; named sites use 720 directions). NASA/JPL SPICE kernels give the position of the Sun and Earth every hour from 2025 to 2030, in the same Moon-fixed frame as the terrain. All of that is packed into about 10 MB of static files, and the browser does the rest: comparing the Sun and Earth with the horizon, the statistics, the date ranking and the heatmaps. There's no backend server, so it loads quickly and there's nothing to crash.

How we checked it

We recomputed NASA's published south pole illumination map (Mazarico et al. 2011, NASA PGDA) for the same 2009-2013 period. Our sunlight map matches it with a correlation of 0.990 (average difference 1.5 percentage points), and our Earth-visibility map matches NASA's at 0.992 (1.8 points). Our Sun and Earth heights agree with JPL Horizons to within about 0.001 degrees. Both comparisons are shown inside the app, so anyone can check them.

Why it matters

Artemis III and the commercial landers heading to the south pole all face the same problem: power and communication depend on timing as much as location. Right now, answering "is the Sun up at this site?" means combining ephemeris queries with a terrain horizon you build yourself. Polaris Window turns hours of that work into a few clicks. It gives planners a quick first look before they move to detailed tools, and gives students and the public an accurate, visual way to see why the south pole is so valuable and so difficult.

What makes it creative

Instead of a static map, it treats landing like a forecast: pick a place, read the outlook, find the best day. You can look at a site's real horizon, rank landing dates instead of just sites, and test whether a lander's battery would survive the night, all in a browser, even on a phone.

What we considered

- Accuracy first: every number comes from NASA data, and we validated against NASA's own maps before building the interface.

- Being honest about limits: the 80 m terrain can't show boulders or small craters. The app explains this with the real IM-2 Athena landing in March 2025, where the site and date were good but the lander tipped over in a small crater. Polaris Window is an educational and planning tool, not NASA-endorsed and not flight-certified.

- Easy to understand: plain-language labels, a short welcome card, a 1-minute guided tour, and a clean black-and-white design that keeps the focus on the data.

- Works anywhere: desktop, tablet and phone, with a small download and no account.

Tools we used

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Numba, SpiceyPy, Matplotlib) for the data pipeline; JavaScript, Three.js and Chart.js for the app; GitHub Pages for hosting; Playwright for testing; and Remotion and FFmpeg for the demo video, with narration generated using ElevenLabs.
